lede: Stations read against the page images of their sources only; each names its source. Links into the modules follow as the modules are printed.

stations.text: The Florida Mortgage and Investment Company announces “a provisional contract … for the purchase of 47,000 acres of freehold land, situate on Sarasota Bay, Manatee County, Florida”; the most delicate vegetables grown there go to the northern markets in January and February, “as the lands are below the frost line”.

A witness at the trial for the murder of Harrison T. Riley tells of a meeting in Jason Alford's house on the Saturday night before the killing: “That was a meeting of an organization known as the Sara Sota Vigilance Committee, styled S. S. V. C.”
stations.quelle: Bacon, Andrews and Bidwell v. State, 22 Fla. 51 (January term 1886), p. 64.

stations.text: Charles E. Abbe is killed by a shotgun shot to the head; Florida's Supreme Court later finds the killing premeditated and upholds the conviction of Joseph C. Anderson as present, aiding and abetting.

A colonist remembers: “About January 9 it became much colder and snow began to fall, greatly to the surprise of the natives who thought at first the woods were afire and that the ashes were being carried by the wind.”
stations.quelle: Memoirs of Alex Browning, as quoted in Karl H. Grismer, The Story of Sarasota (1946), p. 97.

stations.text: A directory of the people living in what became Sarasota County lists the residents of Sarasota by name. “Six colored persons also were listed: J. Coleman, Lewis Colson, E. Justice, John Mays, and I. P. and W. S. Washington.”
stations.quelle: Grismer, The Story of Sarasota (1946), p. 131, after a directory of 1897.

stations.text: At a mass meeting in Harry L. Higel's office on the wharf the village votes to incorporate as a town. “Practically every qualified voter in the village attended—53 of them.”
stations.quelle: Grismer, The Story of Sarasota (1946), p. 136.

stations.titel: The circus man buys a home
stations.text: John Ringling, fishing in the Sarasota section, buys the winter home of C. N. Thompson, “said to be one of the finest places in that section of the State”.
stations.quelle: Tampa Times, 28 August 1911, reprinted in the Manatee River Journal, 31 August 1911, p. 1.

stations.text: On 33rd Street, outside the town, Black families build “tiny homes” in Newtown, opened by Charles N. Thompson. “Previously, their principal living quarters had been at Black Bottom, in the vicinity of 12th and Lemon.”
stations.quelle: Grismer, The Story of Sarasota (1946), p. 179.

stations.text: J. R. Bunkley, “former convict guard, who is being held for the murder of a negro prisoner at Salt Springs”, is bound over on a bond of $5,000 until the grand jury of Sarasota County meets. In the same week the Governor appoints the officials of the new county.
“Approximately 150 local Klansmen attended the circus in full Klan regalia. A huge Klan parade was held immediately before the start of the evening's program.”

stations.titel: A hotel for the colored tourist trade
stations.text: E. O. Burns announces a $15,000 hotel on Central near Fourteenth Street that “will cater to the colored tourist trade”, to be named for Louis Colson, who had worked in the home of J. H. Gillespie and died about two years before.

Drained from 1924 and first planted in January 1927, Palmer Farms sends its first shipment: three cars of tomatoes and one of potatoes. It later turns to celery; by 1946 “70 per cent of those employed are negroes”.
stations.quelle: Grismer, The Story of Sarasota (1946), p. 256.

stations.text: The census counts 8,398 people in the city of Sarasota, against 2,149 in 1920 and 840 in 1910, and 12,440 in Sarasota County.
stations.quelle: Fifteenth Census of the United States: 1930, Population, vol. I, Florida, table 4, p. 213.

stations.text: The Army air base, a bomber base from the spring of 1942 and then a fighter base with more than 3,000 men at its peak, is inactivated; the following month the government turns it back to the Airport Authority.
stations.quelle: Grismer, The Story of Sarasota (1946), p. 250.
